stem: During infusion of a vesicant antineoplastic drug, the client reports burning and swelling at the IV site. Why is this finding urgent?

options.A: Vesicant extravasation usually causes only transient skin discoloration without deeper tissue injury.
options.B: Burning at the site confirms a systemic allergic reaction rather than a local infusion complication.
options.C: Tissue injury is unlikely once the IV catheter is in a peripheral vein, so the infusion can continue while the site is observed.
options.D: Vesicant extravasation can cause severe local tissue injury, including necrosis, so the infusion complication requires prompt recognition and management.

rationale: NCBI StatPearls defines a vesicant as a drug that can cause tissue necrosis if it extravasates into subcutaneous tissue. Reported complications include pain, burning, stinging, erythema, sudden edema, and tissue necrosis. Management begins with stopping vesicant administration after extravasation is confirmed. Therefore burning and swelling during a vesicant infusion are urgent because serious local tissue injury can occur; D is correct.
educational_objective: Recognize burning and swelling during vesicant infusion as possible extravasation with risk of tissue necrosis requiring prompt management.
source_version_date: StatPearls 2026 edition; article last updated February 27, 2023; live applicability rechecked August 16, 2026
source_locator: Other Issues > Complications of Extravasation of Vesicants and Management: vesicants can cause tissue necrosis after extravasation; complications include pain, burning, stinging, erythema, sudden edema and tissue necrosis; management begins by stopping vesicant administration after confirmation.
source_claim_supported: Burning and swelling during vesicant infusion are concerning for extravasation, which can cause serious local injury including tissue necrosis and requires prompt management.

options.A: Vesicant extravasation usually causes only transient skin discoloration without deeper tissue injury.
options.B: Burning at the site confirms a systemic allergic reaction rather than a local infusion complication.

source_original.rationale: Vesicant extravasation can produce pain, swelling and serious local injury, including tissue necrosis. Prompt recognition and management are needed to limit damage.

correction_summary: Retained the vesicant-extravasation construct and key D, explicitly linked the urgency to recognized extravasation symptoms and necrosis risk, and reduced difficulty from hard to medium because the final item tests a direct complication-recognition principle.

audit_findings.source_authority: NCBI/StatPearls current 2026 edition; NCSBN 2026 Test Plan
audit_findings.currentness: StatPearls article last updated 2023-02-27 and present in 2026 edition; applicability live-rechecked 2026-08-16
audit_findings.exact_locator: StatPearls Complications of Extravasation of Vesicants and Management; NCSBN Physiological Adaptation printed p.14 rendered and verified
audit_findings.claim_audit: Final item accurately links burning/swelling to possible extravasation and necrosis risk without overclaiming that symptoms alone prove a specific drug injury severity.

distractor_audit.A: Incorrect because vesicant extravasation can progress to deep tissue necrosis.
distractor_audit.B: Incorrect because local burning/swelling are recognized extravasation manifestations and do not confirm systemic allergy.
distractor_audit.C: Incorrect because peripheral IV placement does not eliminate extravasation risk and continued vesicant infusion can worsen injury.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only D explains the recognized urgent local complication and its potential severity.
audit_findings.cueing: All alternatives interpret the same local infusion findings; D was kept concise and clinically specific.
audit_findings.blueprint: Physiological Adaptation — recognize acute complications and intervene.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Re-read the NCBI extravasation section, NCSBN Physiological Adaptation screenshot, stem/options/rationale/objective, ambiguity and cueing. D remained uniquely correct.
